Notes: First documented Jewish settler: Samuel Hirschberg arrived in Oakland in 1852 (town then ~1,000 residents) and ran a dry-goods store; individual presence
Beth Jacob history: Jewish settlers had already arrived when Oakland received its city charter in 1854; presence without count
Oakland Hebrew Benevolent Society established by 14 leading Jewish citizens of Oakland for religious and charitable needs; organized community (14 = founders subset)
Hebrew Benevolent Society organized by eighteen merchants and shopkeepers, predominantly Polish Jews from Poznan; founders subset
First Jewish organization: Oakland Hebrew Benevolent Society (1862), which owned a cemetery
Eighteen businessmen (immigrants from Germany, Hungary and Poland) form the First Hebrew Congregation of Oakland (now Temple Sinai); founders subset
Oakland lodge of B'nai B'rith founded in 1875; First Hebrew Congregation founded 1875
First synagogue built at 14th and Webster, large enough to hold 500 people (seating capacity not population)
Jewish population of the city in 1880 was 227; a further 68 lived in the suburbs (not included)
First Hebrew Congregation hires its first rabbi, Meyer Solomon Levy
Beth Jacob Congregation (Orthodox) founded 1884 per congregation history; incorporated 19 Dec 1893
Congregation Beth Jacob (Orthodox) founded by Eastern Europeans in 1887 per JVL (date differs from congregation's own history)
Rabbi Shlomo DovBer and Hadasah Goldberg immigrated from Russia to Oakland in 1900; individual presence
Beth Jacob membership 40 members in 1901 (one congregation's membership; not community total)
Jewish Encyclopedia (vol. published 1902; year of data = publication year): Oakland had 2 congregations, 2 benevolent societies, 1 Sabbath school, 2 lodges

AJYB 1917-18 table of cities with >1,000 Jews lists Oakland 227 for 1905 (identical to the 1880 figure; possibly a carried-over estimate) [Review fix: Population 227 moved to Notes - repeats the 1880 figure; likely carried forward]
AJYB 1917-18 table: Oakland 2,000 Jews in 1907 (no figure for 1910 or 1917)
Temple Beth Abraham founded 1907 by Hungarian Orthodox Jews; building at 5th and Harrison Streets
First Hebrew Congregation had 95 members by 1907 (one congregation's membership)
AJYB 1917-18 table: Oakland 3,000 Jews in 1912
Oakland Jewish Relief Federation founded 1918 to centralize Jewish relief work in the East Bay
Chabad Congregation Zemach Zedeck formally incorporated in 1919 (founded by Rabbi Ephraim Garfinkle, who moved to Oakland after 1906 earthquake)
Linfield, Jewish Population of the United States 1927 (AJYB): Oakland total 267,300, Jews 6,000 (2.24%); nearby Piedmont listed separately with 150
Beth Jacob listed a membership of 95 in 1927 (one congregation's membership)
AJYB 1945-46 Table X: Oakland 7,415 Jews (1937 estimates); city total 302,163 (1940 census)
Linfield, Jewish Communities of the United States (1936-37 Census of Religious Bodies): Oakland 7,415 Jews
AJYB 1945-46 Table X: local estimate for Oakland 6,500 Jews in 1942
Oakland Jewish Center built in 1958
Temple Beth Abraham had nearly 700 family members by the late 1960s (one congregation; year = midpoint of 'late 1960s')
Metropolitan Jewish population (incl. Alameda and Contra Costa Counties) of Oakland was 18,000 - metro aggregate, not city
Bay Area Jewish population ~223,000 in the mid-1980s (4% of Bay Area) - regional aggregate; year = mid-1980s
Temple Sinai membership over 640 families by 1993 (one congregation)
Estimated metropolitan Jewish population (incl. Alameda and Contra Costa Counties) of the East Bay 60,000-80,000 - metro aggregate
2011 East Bay Jewish Community Study: Oakland-Berkeley Corridor (multi-city zip region) 64,220 Jews and non-Jews in Jewish households; ~175,000 in whole East Bay - regional aggregates
Temple Sinai had nearly 1,000 member families as of 2015 (one congregation)
